History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
31-year-old man with past history of eczema presents with a 4-day history of intensely pruritic, erythematous, dry/cracked rash on chest, hands, and inner elbows; clinician’s impression is an atopic dermatitis flare, and plans include prescription-strength topical steroid, emollient therapy, and oral antihistamine with follow-up in one week.

History:
• Presenting complaint ­– “very itchy,” red, sore skin rash disturbing sleep and concentration at work.  
• Onset/progression – began 4 days ago; persistent, no improvement despite OTC measures.  
• Location – chest, dorsal/volar hands, inner elbows; no facial, leg, or back involvement.  
• Character – severe pruritus; skin feels “cracked”; no bleeding, pus, or discharge.  
• Relieving/aggravating factors – frequent showers give transient relief; OTC steroid cream and antihistamines provided no relief.  
• Associated symptoms – denies fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, GI or urinary changes.  
• System review (pertinent negatives) – no systemic constitutional symptoms; no respiratory or bowel/urinary complaints; sleep disturbed by itching.

Past Medical History:
• Atopic eczema – prior limited to arms; current widespread flare.  
• Asthma (history) – resolved; no current treatment.  
Medications:  
• OTC topical steroid cream – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• OTC antihistamines – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
Allergies: None reported.

Social History:
• Lives with several flat-mates.  
• Occupation – project manager at pharmaceutical company.  
• Smoking – never smoker.  
• Alcohol – a few beers per week; previously drank more.  
• Recreation – enjoys hiking but currently limited by rash.  
• Financial/lifestyle – shares housing to save money.

Family History:
• Not discussed / not documented.

Physical Examination:
(Virtual inspection)  
• Rash observed by clinician; described only as “familiar,” dry/cracked and erythematous on reported areas.  
• No documented vitals or other system findings.

Investigations:
• None performed or recorded.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Suspected atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare  
  • Assessment: History of eczema; intense pruritus; flexural involvement; dry/cracked skin; no systemic signs of infection.  
  • Plan:  
    – Prescribe higher-potency topical corticosteroid (exact agent/strength not specified).  
    – Prescribe emollient for bath/shower use; advise generous, regular application.  
    – Start oral antihistamine (Fexofenadine) for itch control.  
    – Educate on daily skin hydration, avoiding hot showers and harsh soaps.  
    – Keep diary of possible triggers (soaps, detergents, clothing).  
    – Follow-up in 1 week if no improvement or sooner if worsening.

Issue 2 – Possible allergic/irritant contact dermatitis trigger  
  • Assessment: Acute onset; new distribution; uncertain exposure history.  
  • Plan:  
    – Reinforce trigger diary.  
    – Review any new personal-care products, clothing or environmental exposures.  
    – Consider patch testing if symptoms persist despite eczema-directed therapy (discussion deferred).

Issue 3 – Symptom control and monitoring  
  • Assessment: Severe pruritus causing sleep/work impairment.  
  • Plan:  
    – Continue antihistamine at bedtime if daytime drowsiness occurs.  
    – Counsel on gentle, fragrance-free skin products.  
    – Safety-net: seek care promptly for spreading erythema, pain, discharge, or systemic symptoms.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare – High likelihood: prior history, flexural pattern, dry/cracked skin, intense itch.  
2. Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis – Moderate likelihood: abrupt onset, involvement of exposed areas; unknown new exposure.  
3. Scabies infestation – Low to moderate likelihood: severe pruritus, hand involvement, shared living; no burrows or contacts affected reported (conflict noted: not raised in consult).

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected: objective rash description (morphology, extent), vital signs, detailed family history, complete medication list with dosages.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Occasional audio dropouts; overall intelligible though some statements vague.
